newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Citibank cashes in on Asia's credit-hungry market.
newsitem.headline: Citibank cashes in on Asia's credit-hungry market.

text.p: Citibank is reaping rich dividends in the Philippines and other Asian markets where its credit card business is growing at robust rates, a senior bank official said on Monday.

Business in the Philippines was booming with growth rates seen at 30 percent to 40 percent annually, Harpal Dugal, vice president and business manager for Citibank Philippines credit card divison, told Reuters in an interview on Monday.
The growth comes on top of a threefold increase in the size of the business in the past three years.
Total annual spending in the Philippines through credit cards had risen to between 45 billion pesos ($1.72 billion) and 50 billion pesos annually from 16 billion to 18 billion pesos in 1993, he said.
Citibank Philippines, a unit of Citicorp, dominates the business with its cards accounting for 14 to 15 billion pesos out of a total spending of 45 to 50 billion pesos.

Dugal declined to give profit figures for Citibank's credit card business in the Philippines but said it accounted for about 65 to 70 percent of profits in its consumer banking division and about 30 to 35 percent of total profits.
Industry analysts said Citibank Philippines credit card division's profits had grown 10-fold in the past three years.
Dugal said Citibank's Philippine experience was replicated in most Asian countries.
Myths about Asians being conservative and reluctant to leverage on future earnings were simply not true, he said.
"In most countries in Asia, you'll find revolving rates much in excess of 65 to 70 percent," Dugal said.
The credit-revolving rate is the amount of money on which credit card users pay interest because they have not paid their dues within the stipulated time of one month.
The hunger for unsecured credit has been tempered despite the fact that interest rates on revolving credit range from between 33 and 45 percent.
"That myth (that Asians are relectant to be in debt) has been shattered ... irrespective of cultures and ethnicity and religion, (it is) the same pattern all over Asia," Dugal said.
"We are talking about the global customer, whether he is in Asia or the Middle East."
Dugal said of Citibank's worldwide 1995 profits of over $3.0 billion, 30 to 35 percent may have come from credit cards.
He said Citibank did not have any serious multinational competitor in Asia because it was the first to enter the market about seven years ago.
"It is only recently that some of the multinational banks have started pan-Asian efforts, especially Amex (American Express), Chartered and recently Hongkong Bank," he said.
Dugal said an important factor for the growth of credit cards was that unsecured credit was not easily available.
"Unofficial lenders, their rates are 50 or 60 percent and banks for some reason are not offering consumer unsecured credit at rates of 25 and 35 percent, he said.
He predicted banks would soon try to cash in on the unsecured loans market. "I believe (this) will happen in this market going forward," he said.
